items.prompt: Which organ does a bird sing with?

options.label: The syrinx
options.feedback: It sits deep in the chest, where the windpipe divides.

options.label: The larynx
options.feedback: That is your voice box. A bird has one, and it is silent.

options.label: The tongue
options.feedback: It shapes some sounds; it makes none.

options.label: The crop
options.feedback: A storage pouch for food, with no part in sound.

items.ok_line: Not a throat at all — the sound starts in the chest.
items.ko_line: Whatever a bird sings with, it is not the organ you speak with.
items.exp_title: A voice where the windpipe forks
items.exp_text: Birds have a larynx but do not sing with it. Their voice is the syrinx, a chamber sitting at the very bottom of the windpipe where it splits towards the two lungs. Membranes there vibrate as air passes, and small muscles tune them. Being buried in the chest and surrounded by an air sac, it converts breath to sound with remarkable efficiency — some birds turn nearly all of it into noise, where a person wastes most.

items.prompt: How can some birds sing two different notes at the same time?

options.label: Their voice has two independent sides
options.feedback: One for each branch of the windpipe, controlled separately.

options.label: They sing while breathing in and out
options.feedback: That sustains a song, but gives one note at a time.

options.label: The second note echoes off the throat
options.feedback: An echo repeats a note; it does not add a new one.

options.label: Two birds are usually singing together
options.feedback: A single recorded bird produces both notes.

items.ok_line: One instrument with two halves, played independently.
items.ko_line: The clue is where the syrinx sits — right where one tube becomes two.
items.exp_text: Because the syrinx sits at the fork of the windpipe, it has a membrane on each branch, and many songbirds drive the two separately. A wood thrush can sing a rising phrase with one side while the other sings a falling one, harmonising with itself. Some species divide the labour by pitch: low notes from the left, high from the right, switched so fast the join cannot be heard.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a bird's song and its call?

options.label: A song claims territory or a mate
options.feedback: Long and elaborate. Calls are short and practical.

options.label: A song is simply louder
options.feedback: An alarm call often carries further than any song.

options.label: A call is used only by young birds
options.feedback: Adults call constantly, all year round.

options.label: A song is used only in flight
options.feedback: Most birds sing from a perch, deliberately exposed.

items.ok_line: The song advertises. The call does business.
items.ko_line: Ask what each one is *for*, rather than how it sounds.
items.exp_text: A song is long, structured, usually seasonal, and delivered from a conspicuous perch: it announces that this ground is taken and that the singer is worth pairing with. Calls are short and used all year — contact notes to keep a flock together, alarms, begging by chicks. Alarms are often thin high whistles that are hard to place, so the caller does not give itself away while warning everyone else.

items.prompt: Are birds born knowing their song?

options.label: Many must learn it from an adult
options.feedback: Reared in silence, they produce something barely recognisable.

options.label: All of them are born knowing it
options.feedback: That holds for some groups, but not for songbirds.

options.label: They copy whatever they hear as adults
options.feedback: Most species can only learn during a short early window.

options.label: They invent it fresh each season
options.feedback: A bird's song stays remarkably stable year to year.

items.ok_line: Song is inherited as a rough sketch and learnt as a finished thing.
items.ko_line: Raise a chaffinch where it hears no adult and listen to the result.
items.exp_title: A sketch inherited, the detail learnt
items.exp_text: A chaffinch raised in silence sings something with the right length and pitch range but none of the structure. Given recordings during its first months, it produces the real song. There is a window: hear nothing then, and the chance is gone. Young birds even babble a rambling subsong before settling on the adult version, and the parallel with a child learning to speak is close enough that the same brain circuits are studied side by side.

items.prompt: Which bird is the most accomplished mimic?

options.label: The lyrebird
options.feedback: It reproduces other species, and machinery, with startling accuracy.

options.label: The nightingale
options.feedback: A famous singer, but its song is its own.

options.label: The blackbird
options.feedback: It borrows the odd phrase and no more.

options.label: The skylark
options.feedback: Long and complex, yet entirely original.

items.ok_line: It copies anything it hears often enough, living or not.
items.ko_line: The bird is Australian, and its tail is as famous as its voice.
items.exp_text: A male superb lyrebird spends most of his display copying other species — twenty or more in one performance, each accurate enough to fool the bird being imitated. Individuals have been recorded reproducing camera shutters, car alarms and chainsaws. Because young males learn from older ones, a copied sound can outlive its source: lyrebirds in one region kept a flute-like phrase circulating for decades after the source had gone.

items.prompt: Why do birds sing most intensely at dawn?

options.label: Sound travels furthest in the still air
options.feedback: Cool, calm air carries a song several times as far.

options.label: They are hungriest at first light
options.feedback: Hunger sends a bird to feed, not to a perch.

options.label: The light hurts their eyes
options.feedback: Nothing about dawn light troubles a bird.

options.label: Predators cannot hear at dawn
options.feedback: Hunters hear perfectly well at any hour.

items.ok_line: The same effort buys far more ground at first light.
items.ko_line: Ask what is different about the air itself before the sun warms it.
items.exp_title: The hour when a voice carries
items.exp_text: Before the sun stirs the air, there is little wind and no rising turbulence to scatter sound; a song can carry as much as twenty times further than at midday. The light is still too poor for catching insects, so the time is worth little for feeding. Each species has its own place in the queue — robins and blackbirds first, later risers after — so the dawn chorus arrives in a fairly fixed order.

items.prompt: Which bird makes the loudest call yet recorded?

options.label: The white bellbird
options.feedback: About 125 decibels, painful at close range.

options.label: The peacock
options.feedback: Piercing and far-carrying, but nowhere near that.

options.label: The great horned owl
options.feedback: Its hoot travels far by being low, not loud.

options.label: The herring gull
options.feedback: Loud enough to wake a town, and still far behind.

items.ok_line: Louder at a metre than a pneumatic drill.
items.ko_line: The record holder is a small white bird of the Amazon.
items.exp_title: A shout from a bird the size of a pigeon
items.exp_text: The white bellbird of the Amazon was measured at around 125 decibels — louder than a chainsaw, from a bird weighing about 250 grams. It has unusually thick abdominal muscles and ribs, apparently to drive the air. The strangest part is the delivery: the male aims his loudest call directly at a female perched beside him, turning to face her first. She chooses to stay for it.

items.prompt: What is a dialect in birdsong?

options.label: A local version of a species' song
options.feedback: Valleys apart can sing recognisably differently.

options.label: The song of a young bird
options.feedback: That is subsong, and it is a stage rather than a place.

options.label: A song used only in winter
options.feedback: Most birds barely sing outside the breeding season.

options.label: A call shared between two species
options.feedback: Species may copy each other, but that is mimicry.

items.ok_line: Same species, different neighbourhood, different accent.
items.ko_line: The word means the same for birds as it does for people.
items.exp_text: Because young birds copy the adults around them, small differences accumulate wherever populations rarely mix, and neighbouring valleys can end up singing distinguishable versions. White-crowned sparrows around San Francisco Bay hold dialects that shift within a few kilometres. Females often prefer the local accent, so the boundary reinforces itself — the first step, over long enough, towards two species that no longer answer each other.

items.prompt: In Europe, which birds usually do the singing?

options.label: Mostly the males
options.feedback: They hold the territory and advertise for a mate.

options.label: Mostly the females
options.feedback: In the tropics females sing plenty. In Europe, less so.

options.label: Only birds under a year old
options.feedback: Young birds sing worst, not most.

options.label: Only birds that do not migrate
options.feedback: Migrants sing hard on arrival, when time is short.

items.ok_line: In Europe. Elsewhere the answer changes.
items.ko_line: Ask which bird has to claim a patch of ground each spring.
items.exp_title: A northern habit, not a universal rule
items.exp_text: In temperate Europe the male arrives first, claims ground and sings to hold it and attract a mate; the female rarely does. For a century this was written up as how birds work. It turned out to be a local pattern: across the tropics, where pairs hold territory all year, females sing as much as males and often duet with them so precisely that the two sound like one bird. Reconstructions suggest the ancestral songbird female sang.

items.prompt: How do birds in noisy cities make themselves heard?

options.label: They sing higher and louder
options.feedback: Traffic noise is low-pitched, so they climb above it.

options.label: They stop singing altogether
options.feedback: A bird that stops loses its territory.

options.label: They sing only in the rain
options.feedback: Rain adds noise rather than removing it.

options.label: They sing much more slowly
options.feedback: Slowing down does nothing against a constant roar.

items.ok_line: Traffic rumbles low, so the song climbs out of its way.
items.ko_line: Traffic noise sits at the bottom of the range. Where would you go?
items.exp_text: City traffic produces a low-frequency roar, so urban great tits sing at a higher pitch than woodland ones and raise their volume, an adjustment measured in cities across Europe. Some shift their timing instead, starting before the rush hour. It is not free: a higher, shorter song carries less information about the singer, and females in some species find it less attractive.
